Impact of Differences in CACS on Plaque Burden Category Classification There was no evidence of a difference between the P classification of TNC and PureCalcium images (P = .18). The classification was consistent in 125 patients, whereas in 45 patients, there was a discrepancy between PureCalcium and TNC P classifications. On PureCalcium images, 20 patients were misclassified as P1 instead of P0 on TNC images (P < .001). In these patients, the median Agatston score on PureCalcium images was 2.1 (minimum, 0.5; maximum, 4.8). Fourteen patients were misclassified as P0 instead of P1 (P = .07), with a median Agatston score of 3.8 (minimum, 0.5; maximum, 16.6) (Table 3). The categorical agreement of plaque classification between TNC CACS and PureCalcium CACS was excellent (κ = 0.88).

In terms of radiation dose, the mean dose-length product for the entire examination was 233.1 mGy · cm ± 206.8, while the dose-length product for the TNC scan was 32.5 mGy · cm ± 11.5. Therefore, TNC image acquisition contributed 19.7% ± 8.8 of the total radiation dose.

from contrast-enhanced coronary CT angiography for coronary artery calcium scoring (CACS). PureCalcium images from routine CT angiography may obviate the need for a dedicated calcium scoring scan, offering comprehensive information on calcium burden and plaque composition on a single scan while reducing radiation exposure. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test indicated no evidence of a difference in the median Agatston scores between true noncontrast (TNC) and PureCalcium CACS. The analysis revealed excellent correlation between Agatston scores obtained from both techniques. However, the equivalence test proved inconclusive, while agreement between PureCalcium and TNC calcium scores was suboptimal. The findings of our study are consistent with previous research that evaluated the accuracy and reliability of calcium scoring using different imaging techniques. Studies exploring the use of dual-energy CT and virtual noncontrast imaging for coronary calcium quantification demonstrate the potential of these techniques in presenting a good correlation between TNC and virtual noncontrast images for CACS (9,17). The assessment and comparison of virtual noncontrast CT images from a dual-layer spectral detector CT scanner with TNC data found good correlation between CACS data, but significant differences persisted (in the study by Langenbach et al [11], mean difference of 83 and limits of agreement of 196–362; results not given in the study by Gassert et al [8]), restricting the clinical implementation of the approach (8,11). Photon-counting CT has demonstrated its potential to enhance various applications, including CACS, surpassing energy-integrating detector CT (18). Although photon-counting CT theoretically improves material separation, its impact on CACS derived from contrast-enhanced CCTA has not been comprehensively studied.
